blocks.text: Crown Prince Rudolf came into the world as the great hope of the Habsburgs, the long-awaited male heir who was supposed to secure the future of the dynasty. But from the very beginning, there were signs that this boy was not made for the world he had been born into. Even before his birth, a dark shadow seemed to hang over him. On August 16, 1858, the great chandelier in the ceremonial hall of Schönbrunn Palace suddenly crashed to the ground.

Many took it as an evil omen. Five days later, on August 21, in the new castle at Laxenburg, after two daughters, the eagerly awaited son was finally born. Rudolf Franz Karl Josef. The joy at the Viennese court was enormous.

One hundred and one cannon shots announced the birth of the heir to the monarchy. From the very first day, it was clear what role this child was meant to play. In an army order issued on August 22, Franz Joseph declared that the son given to him by God’s grace would belong to his brave army from the moment he entered the world, and he appointed the newborn colonel-in-chief of his 19th Line Infantry Regiment, which would henceforth bear the name Crown Prince. Shortly afterward, the infant received the Order of the Golden Fleece. At his baptism on August 23, he was given the programmatic first name Rudolf, a reference to the founder of the dynasty. Yet despite all the dynastic hopes placed upon him, Rudolf’s childhood was anything but sheltered. Above all, his relationship with his mother was disturbed early on. When Franz Joseph traveled to the Italian theater of war in May 1859, Elisabeth fell into a state of severe agitation. Nervousness, sleeplessness, and an almost compulsive need to move drove her increasingly into her favorite passion: riding. A few weeks before Rudolf’s second birthday, she rushed off to her parents and siblings at Possenhofen in Bavaria. After her return to Austria, her health worsened again. On medical advice, she spent the autumn, winter, and the spring of 1861 on Madeira.

During this time, she wrote letters only to her daughter Gisela. The little Rudolf was deeply hurt by this. Grandmother Sophie described the scene in a letter: Gisela had received a letter from her mother. Rudolf was furious that he had not received one and, in deep indignation, threw a blank sheet of paper on the floor that someone had naively given him as compensation. Elisabeth responded to her son with a letter of her own: My dear Rudolf, I have heard that you were quite angry that I did not write to you as well. I thought you were too small to understand, but you are already quite sensible now. I will bring you many beautiful toys. Do you remember me at all? With heartfelt kisses, your Mama. But when they finally met again in Venice, a scene that a sentimental film later romanticized, it became clear how great the estrangement had already become. Unlike his sister Gisela, Rudolf barely remembered his mother. The unfamiliar surroundings unsettled him, and he was shy with Elisabeth.

The chamberlain who accompanied them reported back to Vienna that the poor Crown Prince often sighed for his nursemaid, felt uncomfortable everywhere, and even had the sorrow to weep and cling to her when Her Majesty wanted him. Franz Joseph tried to defuse the situation and apparently asked the boy to pull himself together for his mother’s sake. The chamberlain noted: The Crown Prince told us he had promised Papa he would not cry anymore when Mama calls. And he kept his word, except for one time when, sobbing, he kept assuring everyone: Actually, I am being very good. Even after the return to Vienna, the situation did not improve. Elisabeth again suffered from fever and coughing fits, and again the doctors advised a long stay in the south. This time to Corfu from July to October. She sent tender letters and small gifts to her children, but the emotional distance had already grown. Rudolf oriented himself more and more toward his father, while Gisela painfully missed her mother. The little boy, by contrast, always wanted to be with his father and constantly asked to go to him at Laxenburg. Later, Rudolf would remember his mother as a mostly sickly, often ill-tempered woman who complained about her ailments. He was not entirely alone, however.

A particularly close bond connected him to his sister Gisela, who lovingly cared for her younger brother. When the children were reunited after a separation, they hugged and kissed each other without pause. In the nursery, there were also important caregivers. Rudolf and Gisela were devoted to their governess, Baroness Charlotte von Welden, and Rudolf had an especially tender relationship with his nurse Leopoldine Nischer. Almost always at his side was his dog Felly. His grandmother, Archduchess Sophie, also cared for her grandchildren constantly and lovingly. She described the little Rudolf as a strong, cheerful, and remarkably well-developed child. In 1859 she wrote to her son Maximilian: Everything is well with us. The little heir is a strikingly strongly developed child, he already sits upright, has fists like a grenadier and a beautiful, full body, a broad, high chest, and like his sister, he is a cheerful, happy child. She described how Gisela would call him over to play and how the two children adored each other. Franz Joseph, too, was an attentive father in the early years, though a strict one. He wanted to pass on to his son the values and interests that had shaped him: the military, riding, hunting.

But early on, it became clear that Rudolf was not at all like his father in temperament. Still, he constantly tried to please him, especially during hunts. After Rudolf’s first stag, Franz Joseph telegraphed with great joy, congratulating him. Such moments showed how much Franz Joseph linked achievement with approval. After every hunt, Rudolf’s gunsmith had to report to the emperor, and the father was mainly interested in how successful his son had been. Rudolf began shooting at the age of eight. Proudly, Franz Joseph wrote that Rudolf shoots squirrels in the garden and rabbits in the pheasantry. The hunter is in his blood.

But soon he doubted whether the ten-year-old Rudolf truly shared the same passion. He admonished him in a letter: I regret very much that despite a promising start you missed everything at the hunt, and I hope only that on future hunts you will shoot better. It is something else to shoot tame animals in a boring park and to bring down real game in the glorious mountains. The main thing is not to lose courage and to go into every hunt convinced that you must hit your target.

Rudolf’s relationship with killing animals remained contradictory all his life. In his childhood drawings, the shot and the bleeding animal were strikingly emphasized. At twelve, he wrote a letter to an eagle he had apparently had in his sights, apologizing for the small offense and signing it faithfully yours until shot, Rudolf, friend of birds. Years later, he confided to an Egyptologist that he took no pleasure at all in hunting red deer and chamois, that killing, especially the mass slaughter of innocent animals, filled him with disgust. Yet the hunting records listed around fifty thousand animals killed by his own hand by the time of his death. A depressing contradiction between personal feeling and courtly expectation. Franz Joseph also tried to raise his son toward hardness and manliness. Having been enthusiastic about everything military in his own childhood, he could not understand why his son might feel differently. Again and again he urged the little Rudolf to be braver. In February 1862, he wrote: You have seen the soldiers of your regiment dance. That must have been very pretty. Only I hear that you were afraid, which is a shame.

Already in May 1862, the three-and-a-half-year-old Rudolf began serious lessons in writing, arithmetic, religion, Hungarian, and Czech. He was considered very intelligent and handled the workload successfully. A deep caesura came when Rudolf was six. He received his own court and was removed from the female world of his childhood, separated from his sister, his governess, and the familiar women of the nursery. This change, normal in the imperial family, hit him hard. On November 1, 1865, Franz Joseph wrote to his mother Sophie: Today the great changes for the children take place. At one-thirty Welden departs, and Rudolf immediately moves in with the gentlemen. So far he is very steadfast. Gisela is already crying a little and will probably become softer at the farewell. From then on, the siblings saw each other only at meals. Different daily routines and separate summer stays increased the distance. From Gisela’s letters, it is clear how much she missed her brother.

She wrote that words could not express how much she thought of him and how slowly time passed without him. Politics also entered Rudolf’s life early. During the conflict of 1866, which led Austria and Prussia into war, the not-yet-eight-year-old crown prince followed events attentively. He was kept informed by his tutors and took a lively part. After Franz Joseph issued his manifesto calling for battle, Rudolf wrote to his father the very next day: My dear Papa, I send you my prayer, which I always say for you in the morning. I have read your manifesto. I liked it very much. And I have also read the manifesto of the King of Prussia. He lies to dear God in the face. I do not like it. The prayer for his father asked almighty God to protect Austria, bless the weapons of its warriors, and watch over his dear Papa in all dangers. After the Austro-Prussian War, an attempt at reconciliation was made.

The parties met in Bad Gastein in August 1871, and since Prince Friedrich Wilhelm of Prussia, the future Kaiser Wilhelm II, and the Austrian heir Rudolf were nearly the same age, they were depicted together in a print as a sign of friendship and harmony. Despite his proximity to the emperor, Rudolf was often lonely. His mother traveled constantly, and his father was absent due to government affairs and military obligations. When Elisabeth stayed in Meran with Gisela and Valerie and Franz Joseph spent several weeks in Budapest, the emperor wrote to his son in November 1870: I regret very much that you must remain so alone in Vienna now and that I cannot keep you company. But you will use this time with your usual sense of duty for diligent study, and Christmas is not far off, when we shall all be reunited. Grandmother Sophie also taught him that a sense of duty must bring comfort. She wrote warmly that fulfilling the task of being his poor Papa’s comfort during the winter would bring its own reward and make him cheerful despite the painful lack of a happy family life. Yet the most consequential episode of his youth was the militaristic education by General Major Leopold Count Gondrecourt. Traditionally, the young crown prince was to be hardened. But Gondrecourt took this idea to extremes. He made Rudolf drill for hours in rain and cold, sometimes woke him with pistol shots, and once abandoned him alone in the forest of the Lainzer Tiergarten. For a sensitive child, this must have been torture.

Contemporaries later reported that this education severely damaged Rudolf’s nerves. Even as an adult, he was said to sleep only with a light on, suffer from sleep disorders, and be prone to anxiety. A liberal politician later judged: His first education, directed by a somewhat limited General Gondrecourt, was very strict and, through exaggerated hardening measures, directly harmful to the child’s nerves. Another contemporary recalled his father’s stories about the draconian methods. According to these accounts, Rudolf once flew into such a rage that he took his rifle, fixed the bayonet, and drove it forcefully through the papered door leading into the room of his tormentor. Notably, reports of Rudolf’s sensitivity and physical weakness became more frequent only from this period onward. After Gondrecourt had been in office for several months, Rudolf’s condition deteriorated so badly that he had to be sent to Ischl for a cure at the end of May. The doctors prescribed him an exact diet and behavior plan: eleven to twelve hours of sleep, fresh spring water upon waking, a light breakfast, a small meal at eleven, dinner at two, and so on, with strict instructions about what fruits were allowed and which were not. When Elisabeth saw her nine-year-old son in Ischl after a long absence, he seemed to her almost dangerously frightened and nervous. She was horrified and delivered her famous ultimatum to Franz Joseph: I wish to retain unrestricted authority over everything concerning the children, the choice of their surroundings, the place of their stay, the complete direction of their education, in a word, everything remains for me alone to determine until the moment of their majority. Interestingly, Gondrecourt had already been stripped of power by then. On May 27, 1865, he was granted leave and did not accompany them to Ischl.

He handed his duties over to Josef Count Latour von Thurnburg. There is no indication that Gondrecourt ever came near Rudolf again. Latour took over Rudolf’s education and deliberately encouraged his natural scientific interests. He was supported by teachers from the bourgeois liberal milieu. This changed Rudolf’s intellectual environment fundamentally. His Hungarian teacher and others introduced him to historical and political ideas that reached far beyond the narrow horizon of the court. The famous animal researcher Alfred Brehm also came to court to teach Rudolf. The crown prince proved eager for knowledge, quick to understand, and extremely keen to learn. Rudolf valued his teachers greatly. But Latour also recognized how sensitive his pupil was. Religious education in particular could shake Rudolf deeply. In a report from December 1868, Latour wrote that Rudolf had tears in his eyes during an examination of conscience.

Before confession, the prince asked for help because he was afraid of overlooking a sin. When the prayer was read aloud, O my God, I have challenged your vengeance against me, I am no longer worthy to be called your child, I have deserved to be eternally cast out by you, the crown prince broke into tears. Latour noted the ambivalence of his feelings, his sins and these words stood in no proper proportion, yet he did not want to make any remark that would change the meaning of the words, fearing the boy would otherwise take the matter too lightly. After the change of teachers, Rudolf’s relationship with his mother also changed. He increasingly saw Elisabeth as an idealized being, almost an angel, and placed blind trust in her. It hit him all the harder when, in 1868, his youngest sister Marie Valerie was born and Elisabeth concentrated almost exclusively on this child. While Gisela accepted the new situation, Rudolf reacted with anger and jealousy. Between him and Valerie, a warm relationship never developed. The year 1872 brought two heavy losses. Rudolf lost his beloved grandmother Sophie. Shortly afterward, his sister Gisela, only sixteen, was married off to a Bavarian relative. A newspaper described Rudolf’s reaction as the most moving sight, he wept continuously and could neither stop his tears nor suppress his sobbing, no matter how hard he visibly struggled for composure.

Despite the marriage, the contact between the siblings remained close. Gisela always assured him that he was warmly invited and welcome at any hour. With the onset of adolescence, other topics came to the fore. His natural history teacher took charge of enlightening the thirteen-year-old Rudolf about sexuality. He first conveyed zoological basics, such as reproduction in animals and the difference between a stallion and a gelding. During a stay in Salzburg, Rudolf visited a fish-breeding facility where the artificial fertilization of fish eggs was explained to him. The teacher reported with satisfaction that His Imperial Highness followed the entire procedure with keen attention. It was added that there was still great uncertainty about the actual process of reproduction in animals and that one should always think and speak of it as one of the deepest and most wonderful secrets of nature. Now an intense, often contradictory interest in women, love, and sexuality awoke in Rudolf. Later notes suggest he sought his first experiences with prostitutes. At the same time, at fifteen, he was infatuated with a girl he knew only from a distance and called Bernardin. The letters to her were never sent.

This already shows a young man painfully aware of the gulf between personal feeling and dynastic duty. He wrote of weeping many tears for her, of great longing and sweet love, but added: My position destroys any relationship with a commoner. I count myself happy to breathe at least the same air as you. But let us hope and trust in God. Before Him, the beggar is equal to the king. Before Him, we are all equal people, whose happiness no rank and no nobility divides. Here, that inner conflict of Rudolf’s becomes visible, the tension between status and feeling, between duty and personal longing. In 1877, his education was officially considered complete. The eighteen-year-old received his own court, and his tutor Latour submitted an account of the expenses of his entire upbringing. A considerable sum of 388,564 guilders and 55 kreuzers. Remarkably, almost a quarter of it had been spent on support, gifts, and tips, an early sign of Rudolf’s pronounced generosity. As a token of recognition for his successfully completed studies, he received the Grand Cross of the Order of Saint Stephen.

But parting from Latour was hard for him. In a letter from July, Rudolf wrote: Dear Latour, this is the first time I take up my pen to write to you, until now we have always been together. It seems so strange to me not to have you always around me. I keep wanting to ask you to come over. And only slowly do I get used to the new life. It is no phrase when I assure you that despite my independence, I was very sad for the first days. The farewell in Schönbrunn would not leave my head. On the hunts I missed you greatly. Thanking you with all my heart for everything, I am your grateful Rudolf. In Latour’s place, Karl Count Bombelles became the new lord chamberlain. He was to accompany Rudolf into a new phase of life, out of school days, into the world of adults. Bombelles reported to Latour that his Crown Prince was doing well physically and mentally, that he never missed an opportunity to mention Latour with the most grateful affection, and that he was gaining his trust daily.

He described how, on the ride from Schönbrunn to Penzing, he told Rudolf to cry it out, that he need not be ashamed of these tears, and the boy did so, opening his heart. Yet Rudolf’s circle now perceived the young man as serious, almost too serious for his age. His former teacher, Baron Walterskirchen, wrote worriedly after seeing a new portrait of Rudolf: The portrait, very nicely executed, shows me that you have become strong and manly. Nevertheless, it cannot fully satisfy me. I miss in it that air of intellectual freshness that always delighted us in you. A gloomy seriousness has settled in your features, which I did not know before. Should life, in the short span since your independence, already stand so cold before your inner eye? For heaven’s sake, do not let the sweet illusions of youth slip away already. They vanish soon enough. It is your duty to preserve your mental freshness for a difficult task. You have a beautiful, joyful youth behind you. You need not gulp down the cup of life in haste.

Enjoy the joy of existence at leisure. You have a right to it, and do not let brooding speculations, whose traces I believe I read in the eyes of your portrait, spoil your joy in living. That you will not drown in the whirlpool of pleasures, for that your mind and your striving for higher things vouchsafe. Rudolf’s childhood and youth already showed everything that would determine his later life: the conflict between duty and personality, between dynastic role and independent thought, between the desire for love and the coldness of the court. From the celebrated heir to the throne did not emerge a second Franz Joseph, but a deeply sensitive, intelligent, and increasingly desperate person who never truly found a home in his own world.
